newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Boosey has no news yet on bid.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Boosey has no news yet on bid.

text.p: Boosey & Hawkes Plc, the British instrument maker and classical music publisher, said on Thursday that it wanted to retain its independence but said it was unaware of any tentative takeover offers being put forward since its biggest shareholder put its 45.3 percent stake up for sale.
Richard Holland, group chief executive, told Reuters in an interview: "My own preference is for the company to remain independent. It's done rather well under that status."
But he added: "There have been no tentative approaches" since its shareholder U.S. music publisher Carl Fischer had made its announcement on Wednesday.
Holland said "Carl Fischer is in the driving seat. It decided to take this decision after lengthy discussions about the options."

He said Boosey was in talks with its advisers about its own choices, but refused to comment on whether it had discussed a possible merger with Carl Fischer or a takeover of Fischer itself, which is a small company. "We have looked at a number of alternatives," said Holland.

Boosey said now that Fischer, its biggest shareholder, had "put up a for-sale sign" the British music group would wait to see what developed. Under London stock market rules, any company making a bid for such a large stake would be obliged to bid for the whole group.

The chief said that Boosey was interested in acquisition-led expansion. Its gearing is between 100 and 115 percent. "I think we've got opportunities for expansion in instruments and publishing. In publishing our interest is in the very serious field of classical music. Not pop, which is a very wide business," he said.

Holland said his group was in a strong position to raise equity for making a large acquisition -- if necessary. "We can fund small deals out of existing borrowings. A larger deal would mean raising more equity but our standing in the market is so high that would be easy to do."

Boosey and Hawkes recently reported a 25 percent hike in pretax profits to 7.70 million stg for 1996. It has delivered compound earnings per share and dividend growth in the last eight years of 20 percent per annum. During that period its market capitalisation increased to 156 million stg from nine million.
Shares in the group were up 25 pence at 892-1/2 pence, after hitting a year high of 905 pence earlier.
-- Edna Fernandes, London newsroom +44 171 542 7717 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
